I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

BODY
Your description names three problems, but they look like one system failing in three places. First, the recurring pattern where you agree on who does something and later disagree about what the agreement meant. My conjecture: the agreements are being made at low resolution. 'Who' gets settled; 'by when', 'how often', and 'what counts as done' get left to assumption, and memory fills the gaps differently for each of you. Second, the changing schedules. Any allocation that was fair when agreed silently decays as shifts move, and staleness feels like unfairness even when nobody broke a promise. Third, the friend who avoids the conversations. My conjecture: this is information about the cost of the conversations, not about the chores. If those talks reliably ended well, he would keep showing up. His absence also means any scheme you and the other friend design over his head will fail the first time it needs his input.

If those conjectures hold, the thing to fix first is not any particular chore but the way agreements get made and refreshed. Concretely: have one conversation about the process itself, not about a current dispute — name the pattern of 'we agreed, then meant different things' and propose changing the format. From then on, write agreements down: task, person, deadline, and what 'done' looks like. A whiteboard or shared note is enough; this removes the whole class of reinterpretation disputes at almost no cost. Put a short, time-boxed check-in on the calendar — fifteen minutes weekly or fortnightly — so schedule changes have a predictable place to land instead of producing surprise resentments. Agree in advance what happens when a chore gets missed: a swap, a trade, a small contribution to a shared pot, so one lapse is an event rather than a verdict on someone's character. And speak to the avoidant friend separately and at low stakes: ask what makes those conversations feel bad, and offer the time-boxed format as the answer rather than pressing him to rejoin the old format.

I would hold all of this loosely. I cannot see whether the real fight is about mismatched standards of clean, about money, or about the friendship itself, and your own part in how the conversations go is invisible from here. The procedural fix only works if the problem is genuinely procedural, and the tests for that are in the commitments.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up involves treating three conjectures as live but unproven: that the reinterpretation disputes are underspecification failures rather than bad faith; that changing schedules make any one-time fair split decay, so a renegotiation rhythm matters more than the initial split; and that the friend's avoidance tracks the felt cost of the conversations. The proposed applications are the written agreement log, the time-boxed check-in, the pre-agreed remedy for missed chores, and the separate low-stakes talk with the avoidant friend. Cheap tests are attached: two to four weeks of written agreements should end the 'that is not what we agreed' disputes if the memory conjecture is right; if they persist in writing, drop that conjecture and redirect toward explicit done-criteria or a renegotiated fairness of the split. If the friend will not attend even a fifteen-minute time-boxed check-in, the procedural reading of his avoidance fails and the problem is likely relational, needing a different kind of conversation entirely. Criticisms I accept in advance: the account rests entirely on one party's report, so the narrator's own contribution to the dynamic goes unexamined; coordination tools do not address standards-mismatch, money, or friendship-level resentment if those are what actually carries the conflict; and the check-in system itself can become one more obligation people shirk. Unresolved: nothing in the exposed material says who is right in any current dispute, and I am not proposing to adjudicate that.

## Selected input rival (p.response.2)

BODY
A rival posing: this may not be an agreement-precision problem but an over-negotiation problem. Where p.rival.0 reads the breakdowns as low-resolution contracts and proposes writing them at higher resolution, I would start from the observation that a shared flat forces friends into dozens of small negotiations a month — who, when, whether it counts — and each one is a fresh chance to argue. Per-instance assignment is itself the conflict generator, and schedule churn multiplies the instances. On this reading, the friend who avoids the conversations is not only telling you the talks are unpleasant; he may have concluded they are pointless, since previous talks produced agreements that decayed. More talk of the same kind will not recruit him.

Three practical consequences follow. First, convert per-task negotiation into standing ownership: divide the shared work into zones (kitchen, bathroom, floors and bins, or whatever fits) with one permanent owner each, balanced by rough minutes rather than perfect fairness, plus a single visible floor-standard per zone agreed once — 'a guest could use this without comment' — instead of renegotiating what 'done' means task by task. Ownership removes most who-and-when negotiation and makes schedule compatibility each owner's private problem. Second, buy out the worst of it: a fortnightly cleaner for the common areas, or any durable cost-shift — a dishwasher, fewer shared meals — aimed specifically at the chores generating the most disputes, split three ways or weighted by income. Resistance to paying is usually symbolic; the flat would be purchasing conflict-reduction, not cleanliness. Third, before redesigning anything for three people, change the one variable you control: for a few weeks, do your own share visibly well, raise nothing mid-dispute, and watch the temperature. This is also diagnostic — if the arguments continue at the same pitch with you fully de-escalated, the fuel lies between the other two or in the arrangement; if it drops, some of it was yours.

I would also treat the avoidance as a fork rather than a symptom: once, one-to-one, ask the absent friend for nothing — 'I'm not asking you to agree to anything; I want to know what living here looks like from your side.' If he talks, you learn which diagnosis you are in. If he won't, the conflict has probably migrated from the chores to the living arrangement itself, and the honest open question becomes whether this configuration of people should keep living together — worth holding in view privately, because it prices the cost of doing nothing. My departure from p.rival.0 is at the level of pose, not of every move: its write-it-down and time-boxed check-in survive inside mine as the floor-standards and a zone-swap review. But I would not expect higher-resolution agreements alone to hold, because the disagreements you describe sound at least partly interest-driven — each of you remembering the favourable version — and documentation does not much restrain motivated compliance.

Everything else — zones, floor-standards, the buyout, the de-escalation trial, the ask-nothing conversation — is proposed application, conditional on the conjectures surviving this flat's history: if flare-ups clustered around handoffs and per-task assignments, my framing gains support; if they cluster around relitigating clearly-remembered or written promises, p.rival.0's does, and I would then retract the pose while keeping the floor-standard idea, imported back into its write-it-down scheme.

Zone ownership depends on surviving the initial minute-balancing negotiation, which can reproduce the original fight once at higher stakes; my only mitigations are time-boxing it, accepting rough equality, and pre-agreeing a swap window after a month.

The ownership scheme's own proposed measure — fewer negotiations after adoption — inherits the problem that 'an argument' has no stable unit across households.

Scope and unresolved problems: everything assumes the three intend to keep cohabiting and that the friend's withdrawal is chore-specific; if it extends wider, none of this applies. I do not resolve whose threshold sets a common-area floor standard when the three differ greatly (the guest-test I gesture at may just entrench the middle standard), whether income-weighting the buyout imports a status asymmetry costing more than the chores did, or how the 'should we still live together' question could be raised aloud without functioning as a threat — I flag it as a consequence to price, not an action I defend. Finally, p.rival.0's commitment field was not supplied to me, so convergence or conflict with its test regime is out of view; my reliance on it is limited to its body as quoted.

  "body": "The account diagnoses well, but several of its parts do not sit well with each other, and in places it treats as cheap what is not cheap.\n\nFirst, an internal tension. The third conjecture says the friend avoids the conversations because of what they cost him, yet the remedy prescribes more structured conversation: a process conversation, a recurring check-in, pre-negotiated remedy talks, plus the separate talk. If the irritant is conversational cost, the program schedules the irritant weekly — time-boxed this time, but recurring and hard to skip. Relatedly, the account iterates on a single allocation mechanism — per-instance negotiated assignment — and never considers the standard alternative of standing domain ownership, where each person owns an area end-to-end, timing is at the owner's discretion, and almost no recurring negotiation is needed at all. The problem text itself is evidence that per-instance negotiation is the failing component; the choice to optimize that mechanism rather than replace it is made without argument, and it is the choice that maximizes dependence on the friend who avoids talking.\n\nSecond, the memory conjecture has a rival the account never engages. \"Memory fills the gaps differently for each of you\" presumes symmetric, honest reconstruction. But reinterpretation disputes in shared flats are often driven by asymmetric tolerance for mess and motivated reading: both parties remember, each reads the agreement toward less work, or one party minds less and waits for the others to fold. Under that rival, writing it down does not end the disputes, it relocates them — to the meaning of the written words and to who holds the burden where the wording runs out. The account's own fallback, explicit done-criteria, assumes chore language can be made exhaustive; it cannot. The proposed test (two to four weeks of written agreements ending the disputes) conflates the two hypotheses, because motivated interpretation predicts persistence with disputes now attached to the text itself.\n\nThird, the tests are weaker than they look. The check-in attendance test is confounded by the account's own second conjecture: if schedules genuinely churn, recurring absence from a fixed meeting is expected for reasons unrelated to the procedural reading, so absenteeism cannot cleanly indict it. And the remedy menu — swaps, trades, the shared pot — presumes the ongoing participation of the member the diagnosis identifies as least likely to participate. The hardest realistic case is not refusal to attend but assent followed by non-performance: agreements get written and then ignored. Nothing in the account binds that case.\n\nFourth, sequencing and cost. On the account's own epistemics, the cheapest and most diagnostic step — the low-stakes separate talk — should come first, since its outcome decides which of the three conjectures even applies; instead it is fifth, after steps that assume the conjectures hold.   "body": "A rival posing: this may not be an agreement-precision problem but an over-negotiation problem. Where p.rival.0 reads the breakdowns as low-resolution contracts and proposes writing them at higher resolution, I would start from the observation that a shared flat forces friends into dozens of small negotiations a month — who, when, whether it counts — and each one is a fresh chance to argue. Per-instance assignment is itself the conflict generator, and schedule churn multiplies the instances. On this reading, the friend who avoids the conversations is not only telling you the talks are unpleasant; he may have concluded they are pointless, since previous talks produced agreements that decayed. More talk of the same kind will not recruit him.

Three practical consequences follow. First, convert per-task negotiation into standing ownership: divide the shared work into zones (kitchen, bathroom, floors and bins, or whatever fits) with one permanent owner each, balanced by rough minutes rather than perfect fairness, plus a single visible floor-standard per zone agreed once — 'a guest could use this without comment' — instead of renegotiating what 'done' means task by task. Ownership removes most who-and-when negotiation and makes schedule compatibility each owner's private problem. Second, buy out the worst of it: a fortnightly cleaner for the common areas, or any durable cost-shift — a dishwasher, fewer shared meals — aimed specifically at the chores generating the most disputes, split three ways or weighted by income. Resistance to paying is usually symbolic; the flat would be purchasing conflict-reduction, not cleanliness. Third, before redesigning anything for three people, change the one variable you control: for a few weeks, do your own share visibly well, raise nothing mid-dispute, and watch the temperature. This is also diagnostic — if the arguments continue at the same pitch with you fully de-escalated, the fuel lies between the other two or in the arrangement; if it drops, some of it was yours.

I would also treat the avoidance as a fork rather than a symptom: once, one-to-one, ask the absent friend for nothing — 'I'm not asking you to agree to anything; I want to know what living here looks like from your side.' If he talks, you learn which diagnosis you are in. If he won't, the conflict has probably migrated from the chores to the living arrangement itself, and the honest open question becomes whether this configuration of people should keep living together — worth holding in view privately, because it prices the cost of doing nothing. My departure from p.rival.0 is at the level of pose, not of every move: its write-it-down and time-boxed check-in survive inside mine as the floor-standards and a zone-swap review. But I would not expect higher-resolution agreements alone to hold, because the disagreements you describe sound at least partly interest-driven — each of you remembering the favourable version — and documentation does not much restrain motivated compliance.",

## Original problem (task)
[d31d61f36df18c74] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.response.0)
[7117367371213428] (h005.fork5.p.response.0)
Source account: daily/mini_prose/cycle-1/account; selected view: both
Artifact: 7574b53dd2e5edee4e0c0471a64ef3afeef8c7414cc0a16aa99438c812de13ee

BODY
Your description names three problems, but they look like one system failing in three places. First, the recurring pattern where you agree on who does something and later disagree about what the agreement meant. My conjecture: the agreements are being made at low resolution. 'Who' gets settled; 'by when', 'how often', and 'what counts as done' get left to assumption, and memory fills the gaps differently for each of you. Second, the changing schedules. Any allocation that was fair when agreed silently decays as shifts move, and staleness feels like unfairness even when nobody broke a promise. Third, the friend who avoids the conversations. My conjecture: this is information about the cost of the conversations, not about the chores. If those talks reliably ended well, he would keep showing up. His absence also means any scheme you and the other friend design over his head will fail the first time it needs his input.

If those conjectures hold, the thing to fix first is not any particular chore but the way agreements get made and refreshed. Concretely: have one conversation about the process itself, not about a current dispute — name the pattern of 'we agreed, then meant different things' and propose changing the format. From then on, write agreements down: task, person, deadline, and what 'done' looks like. A whiteboard or shared note is enough; this removes the whole class of reinterpretation disputes at almost no cost. Put a short, time-boxed check-in on the calendar — fifteen minutes weekly or fortnightly — so schedule changes have a predictable place to land instead of producing surprise resentments. Agree in advance what happens when a chore gets missed: a swap, a trade, a small contribution to a shared pot, so one lapse is an event rather than a verdict on someone's character. And speak to the avoidant friend separately and at low stakes: ask what makes those conversations feel bad, and offer the time-boxed format as the answer rather than pressing him to rejoin the old format.

I would hold all of this loosely. I cannot see whether the real fight is about mismatched standards of clean, about money, or about the friendship itself, and your own part in how the conversations go is invisible from here. The procedural fix only works if the problem is genuinely procedural, and the tests for that are in the commitments.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up involves treating three conjectures as live but unproven: that the reinterpretation disputes are underspecification failures rather than bad faith; that changing schedules make any one-time fair split decay, so a renegotiation rhythm matters more than the initial split; and that the friend's avoidance tracks the felt cost of the conversations. The proposed applications are the written agreement log, the time-boxed check-in, the pre-agreed remedy for missed chores, and the separate low-stakes talk with the avoidant friend. Cheap tests are attached: two to four weeks of written agreements should end the 'that is not what we agreed' disputes if the memory conjecture is right; if they persist in writing, drop that conjecture and redirect toward explicit done-criteria or a renegotiated fairness of the split. If the friend will not attend even a fifteen-minute time-boxed check-in, the procedural reading of his avoidance fails and the problem is likely relational, needing a different kind of conversation entirely. Criticisms I accept in advance: the account rests entirely on one party's report, so the narrator's own contribution to the dynamic goes unexamined; coordination tools do not address standards-mismatch, money, or friendship-level resentment if those are what actually carries the conflict; and the check-in system itself can become one more obligation people shirk. Unresolved: nothing in the exposed material says who is right in any current dispute, and I am not proposing to adjudicate that.

## Selected input objection (p.response.1)

The account diagnoses well, but several of its parts do not sit well with each other, and in places it treats as cheap what is not cheap.

First, an internal tension. The third conjecture says the friend avoids the conversations because of what they cost him, yet the remedy prescribes more structured conversation: a process conversation, a recurring check-in, pre-negotiated remedy talks, plus the separate talk. If the irritant is conversational cost, the program schedules the irritant weekly — time-boxed this time, but recurring and hard to skip. Relatedly, the account iterates on a single allocation mechanism — per-instance negotiated assignment — and never considers the standard alternative of standing domain ownership, where each person owns an area end-to-end, timing is at the owner's discretion, and almost no recurring negotiation is needed at all. The problem text itself is evidence that per-instance negotiation is the failing component; the choice to optimize that mechanism rather than replace it is made without argument, and it is the choice that maximizes dependence on the friend who avoids talking.

Second, the memory conjecture has a rival the account never engages. "Memory fills the gaps differently for each of you" presumes symmetric, honest reconstruction. But reinterpretation disputes in shared flats are often driven by asymmetric tolerance for mess and motivated reading: both parties remember, each reads the agreement toward less work, or one party minds less and waits for the others to fold. Under that rival, writing it down does not end the disputes, it relocates them — to the meaning of the written words and to who holds the burden where the wording runs out. The account's own fallback, explicit done-criteria, assumes chore language can be made exhaustive; it cannot. The proposed test (two to four weeks of written agreements ending the disputes) conflates the two hypotheses, because motivated interpretation predicts persistence with disputes now attached to the text itself.

Third, the tests are weaker than they look. The check-in attendance test is confounded by the account's own second conjecture: if schedules genuinely churn, recurring absence from a fixed meeting is expected for reasons unrelated to the procedural reading, so absenteeism cannot cleanly indict it. And the remedy menu — swaps, trades, the shared pot — presumes the ongoing participation of the member the diagnosis identifies as least likely to participate. The hardest realistic case is not refusal to attend but assent followed by non-performance: agreements get written and then ignored. Nothing in the account binds that case.

Fourth, sequencing and cost. On the account's own epistemics, the cheapest and most diagnostic step — the low-stakes separate talk — should come first, since its outcome decides which of the three conjectures even applies; instead it is fifth, after steps that assume the conjectures hold. The concession in the commitments that the narrator's own contribution is invisible cuts deeper than the account allows: combined with the avoidance-as-cost conjecture, it leaves open that part of the cost the friend avoids is the narrator, and convening process reform before probing that builds on sand. Finally, "almost no cost" does not survive inspection: someone must administer the log, convene the check-in, and enforce the remedies, and that someone will be the narrator — a managerial role apt to generate exactly the role-resentment the system is meant to dissolve, with the added risk that a written ledger among friends reads as assembling a case file.

My objection could itself be mistaken. Ownership allocation also needs an initial negotiation the avoider may refuse, so it inherits the bootstrapping problem rather than escaping it; and if the disputes really are only about ambiguity, the written-log fix may be exactly right and my alternatives beside the point.
COMMITMENTS
Taking up this objection means treating four criticisms as live but unproven. (1) The claimed tension between a conversation-cost diagnosis and a conversation-heavy remedy commits me to the existence and feasibility of lower-conversation architectures such as standing domain ownership; it loses force if per-instance negotiation is failing only at the level of wording rather than as a mechanism, and I concede the ownership alternative inherits the account's own bootstrapping problem since it too requires an initial negotiation the avoider may refuse. (2) The motivated-interpretation and asymmetric-tolerance rival is a conjecture resting on facts not exposed in the problem text; a cheap discriminator is available — disputes over the meaning of specific written items support the rival, while disputes about whether anything was agreed support the memory conjecture — and my sequencing criticism, if applied by moving the separate low-stakes talk first, would itself produce evidence for or against the rival. (3) The confounding criticism of the attendance test commits me to claiming the account's tests are weakly identifying until schedule constraints are ruled out, not to claiming its conjectures are false. (4) The sequencing and administration-cost claims depend on the narrator's actual role in the flat dynamic and on who would run the proposed system; these cannot be verified from the exposed material, so adopting them means asking rather than asserting. Criticisms I accept in advance: the account already hedges its program and disclaims adjudicating current disputes, so part of my pressure lands on language it qualified; my strategic-behavior framing may overweight calculation against temperament, fatigue, or low mood as causes of avoidance; and nothing here settles whether an alternative architecture fits the flat's money constraints or standards gap, or which flatmate, if any, is in the right.

A rival posing: this may not be an agreement-precision problem but an over-negotiation problem. Where p.rival.0 reads the breakdowns as low-resolution contracts and proposes writing them at higher resolution, I would start from the observation that a shared flat forces friends into dozens of small negotiations a month — who, when, whether it counts — and each one is a fresh chance to argue. Per-instance assignment is itself the conflict generator, and schedule churn multiplies the instances. On this reading, the friend who avoids the conversations is not only telling you the talks are unpleasant; he may have concluded they are pointless, since previous talks produced agreements that decayed. More talk of the same kind will not recruit him.

Three practical consequences follow. First, convert per-task negotiation into standing ownership: divide the shared work into zones (kitchen, bathroom, floors and bins, or whatever fits) with one permanent owner each, balanced by rough minutes rather than perfect fairness, plus a single visible floor-standard per zone agreed once — 'a guest could use this without comment' — instead of renegotiating what 'done' means task by task. Ownership removes most who-and-when negotiation and makes schedule compatibility each owner's private problem. Second, buy out the worst of it: a fortnightly cleaner for the common areas, or any durable cost-shift — a dishwasher, fewer shared meals — aimed specifically at the chores generating the most disputes, split three ways or weighted by income. Resistance to paying is usually symbolic; the flat would be purchasing conflict-reduction, not cleanliness. Third, before redesigning anything for three people, change the one variable you control: for a few weeks, do your own share visibly well, raise nothing mid-dispute, and watch the temperature. This is also diagnostic — if the arguments continue at the same pitch with you fully de-escalated, the fuel lies between the other two or in the arrangement; if it drops, some of it was yours.

I would also treat the avoidance as a fork rather than a symptom: once, one-to-one, ask the absent friend for nothing — 'I'm not asking you to agree to anything; I want to know what living here looks like from your side.' If he talks, you learn which diagnosis you are in. If he won't, the conflict has probably migrated from the chores to the living arrangement itself, and the honest open question becomes whether this configuration of people should keep living together — worth holding in view privately, because it prices the cost of doing nothing. My departure from p.rival.0 is at the level of pose, not of every move: its write-it-down and time-boxed check-in survive inside mine as the floor-standards and a zone-swap review. But I would not expect higher-resolution agreements alone to hold, because the disagreements you describe sound at least partly interest-driven — each of you remembering the favourable version — and documentation does not much restrain motivated compliance.
COMMITMENTS
I am advancing one empirical conjecture (recurring flatmate chore conflict is produced more by the number of negotiations than by their vagueness), one alternative reading of the avoidant friend (concluded-pointlessness rather than conversation-cost — a rival to, not a refutation of, p.rival.0's interpretation), and one interpretive caution (disputes over what an agreement meant are often motivated rather than mnemonic; this is my ground for doubting that documentation alone resolves them, though neither account has evidence for its memory claim from what is exposed). Everything else — zones, floor-standards, the buyout, the de-escalation trial, the ask-nothing conversation — is proposed application, conditional on the conjectures surviving this flat's history: if flare-ups clustered around handoffs and per-task assignments, my framing gains support; if they cluster around relitigating clearly-remembered or written promises, p.rival.0's does, and I would then retract the pose while keeping the floor-standard idea, imported back into its write-it-down scheme.

Zone ownership depends on surviving the initial minute-balancing negotiation, which can reproduce the original fight once at higher stakes; my only mitigations are time-boxing it, accepting rough equality, and pre-agreeing a swap window after a month.

Proposed tests, with weaknesses stated: the de-escalation trial is meant to separate the user's contribution from the system's, but it is unblinded and confounded — schedules change anyway, a few weeks is short, visible restraint can itself read as score-keeping, and bottling legitimate grievances can manufacture a later blow-up that a 'success' reading would misexplain. The ask-nothing one-to-one is meant to discriminate my pointless-talk conjecture from p.rival.0's costly-talk one, but a guarded friend may give a polite non-answer indistinguishable from either, so a null result should count as no evidence. The ownership scheme's own proposed measure — fewer negotiations after adoption — inherits the problem that 'an argument' has no stable unit across households.

Finally, p.rival.0's commitment field was not supplied to me, so convergence or conflict with its test regime is out of view; my reliance on it is limited to its body as quoted.

The sustainability constraint, every offered standing element absorbable by the user alone, transfers costs onto the user by design and is tolerable only if set before resentment accrues, part of why the reservation step precedes everything. Floors at the absorbable level with private upgrades are offered as a partial answer to the open threshold question; I accept the race-to-the-bottom objection and claim only that unilateral upgrade routes blunt it. Keeping dissolution pricing private and pre-set, never uttered, dissolves rather than solves the threat problem; I accept the concealment criticism and hold against it the synthesis's ground that raising it aloud functions as leverage nobody defends — neither horn is cost-free. I rule against income-weighting the buyout on adjudication-avoidance grounds and accept that under sharp pay inequality the unweighted version may be infeasible, which would itself be information about the flat's viability.

Proposed applications in order: the private reservation pricing; the ask-nothing one-to-one; the two-part audit (history, then tally); the time-boxed design conversation conditional on engagement, offering zone ownership, absorbable floors, the one-month swap window, and the infrequent review; the buyout conditional on spare money, the tally landing on the most-disputed chores, and no refusal on principle — unweighted by income, targets set by the tally rather than the payer; the de-escalation trial throughout.

Dependencies accepted: ownership still inherits the objection's bootstrapping concession — one negotiation the avoider may refuse — so engagement gating remains load-bearing; the surviving review still needs a convener, probably the user, so managerial-role and case-file risks shrink further but do not vanish; the account's reminder that the tool can become one more shirked obligation is now internalized as the sustainability constraint rather than merely noted; the whole plan still rests on one party's report and now on one party's record, and if the user is part of the avoided cost, no internal evidence will show it.

Test handles with stated weaknesses: engagement versus refusal of the ask-nothing conversation is diagnostic of implementability, not of motive among the four; a guarded null remains no evidence; 'fewer negotiations' after ownership still lacks a stable unit across households; the tally improves classification without de-biasing the classifier. Unresolved: whether the user's reservation line survives attachment to the actual flatmates; whether lowest-maintainer floors prove acceptable to live in rather than merely acceptable in argument; who is right in any current dispute — still not adjudicated, by design."

Preserve the grounds needed for whatever uptake you propose.\n\n## Original problem (task)\n[d31d61f36df18c74] (h005.task.v1)\nI share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?\n\n## Selected input response (p.carry.0)\n[edd651259f4dd1e6] (h005.fork5.p.carry.0)\nSource response: daily/mini_prose/cycle-1/response; selected view: both\nArtifact: 227e0d9409520b146edb14dce17fd57c83e8c4d0cfccbd16cad71ce4e956fc18\nOriginal body SHA256: 518c62243269d9ddda1ec28f8bbaffa797bd307c51fcaa245fd99ab60c7cc5f2\nOriginal commitments SHA256: 8eaac69591179613e65aaeada15207a09f8aa99970ca68b4d72ba7073e3e3097\nDelivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED\nBODY\nWhere the three pieces leave me: the objection lands on sequencing and cost, the rival lands on mechanism, and what survives of the account is its second conjecture — allocations decay as schedules churn — plus its instinct that agreements need an external home. The account's umbrella claim that this is one system failing in three places also survives, but with the failing component re-identified: not primarily the resolution of agreements but the number of negotiations the arrangement generates.\n\nUse first, ahead of everything else: the rival's ask-nothing conversation, merged with the objection's sequencing point. The account put the separate talk fifth; the objection shows it is the cheapest and most diagnostic step on offer and commits you to nothing; the rival supplies the right form — ask for nothing, learn what living here looks like from his side. Between the three documents there are now four readings of his avoidance on the table: talk is costly, talk has concluded-pointless, temperament or fatigue or low mood (the objection's self-correction, which I adopt), and the possibility that part of the cost is you. A guarded non-answer counts as no evidence, as the rival says. A refusal to have even this conversation moves the problem to the living arrangement itself, which I keep as the priced consequence the rival flags and nobody defends as a move.\n\nSecond, before any redesign: a private retrospective audit, which both critics gesture at. Ask which chores actually generate the disputes, and whether past reinterpretations were about whether anything was agreed or about what agreed words meant. The first is the audit the rival requires for the buyout anyway; the second is the objection's discriminator between the memory conjecture and motivated reading, available at zero cost instead of through a two-to-four-week written-log trial that, as the objection shows, conflates the two hypotheses. The audit is corrupted by the same motivated recall it probes, so it is weak evidence — but cheap, prior, and yours already.\n\nOn mechanism, I revise toward the rival, and the grounds are partly the account's own. Its decay conjecture says per-instance allocations go stale as shifts move; the objection adds that the cure offered — a weekly check-in — schedules the very irritant the account blames for the friend's absence, and that attendance at a fixed meeting is confounded by the same churn. Standing zone ownership with one written floor standard per zone answers decay without recurring negotiation: schedule compatibility becomes each owner's private problem. The objection's bootstrapping concession holds — ownership needs one initial negotiation the avoider may refuse — which is a further reason the design conversation comes after the ask-nothing one, time-boxed, aimed at rough equality with a one-month swap window rather than precision.\n\nWriting survives but changes function. I reject the per-instance agreement log: under motivated interpretation it relocates disputes onto the text, it needs an administrator who will be you, and among friends a ledger can read as assembling a case file. The objection's administration-cost point is decisive here. What remains is the account's kernel — agreements need an external home — shrunk to a few standing standards written once, where the interpretation surface is small and nothing is per-instance.\n\nThe buyout I take conditionally: it is the only proposal whose value is independent of which diagnosis is right, since shrinking the contested surface helps in every world; its dependencies are spare money and the audit landing on the chores actually fought over. The de-escalation trial I take as the only probe of the one variable all three pieces agree is invisible — your own contribution — while reading it as conservatively as the rival instructs: unblinded, short, and a temperature drop implicates you only weakly. What I leave open: which empirical reading of the disputes holds, whether the friend re-engages, the money questions, whose threshold sets the common standard. What I reject: the account's ordering, its 'almost no cost' claim, the weekly check-in as the default rhythm (an infrequent swap review survives inside the ownership architecture), and any remedy menu that presumes the participation of the person the diagnosis marks as least likely to participate. Nothing on offer binds assent-followed-by-non-performance; the escalation ladder ends at whether this configuration of people should keep living together, and it is better to know that in advance than to discover it after building machinery.\nCOMMITMENTS\nCarried as live but unproven: the account's decay conjecture, which I use against its own remedy; the rival's negotiation-count conjecture, still unseparated from the vagueness reading pending the retrospective audit; motivated interpretation as a standing rival to memory, with the caveat that the audit itself is corrupted by the recall bias it probes; and four readings of the friend's avoidance — costly talk, concluded-pointless talk, temperament or low mood, and the user as part of the cost — none eliminated by what is exposed.\n\nProposed applications, in order: the ask-nothing one-to-one first; the private history audit (which chores, and 'never agreed' versus 'meant differently'); one time-boxed design conversation conditional on engagement, offering zone ownership, one written floor standard per zone, rough minute-balancing, and a one-month swap window; a priced buyout aimed at the most-disputed chores, conditional on spare money and on nobody refusing on principle; an infrequent review rather than a weekly check-in; no per-instance ledger; the de-escalation trial running concurrently throughout, read conservatively.\n\nDependencies I accept: ownership inherits the bootstrapping problem the objection concedes — it needs one negotiation the avoider may refuse, hence the sequencing; the surviving review still needs a convener, probably the user, so the managerial-role and case-file risks shrink but do not vanish; a common floor standard may entrench the middle threshold, the rival's own unresolved problem.\n\nTests with stated weaknesses: the retrospective audit is cheap but biased; a guarded null from the ask-nothing conversation is no evidence; 'fewer negotiations' after ownership has no stable unit across households; a temperature drop under de-escalation is confounded, and bottling legitimate grievances can manufacture a later blow-up that a success reading would misexplain.\n\nCriticisms accepted in advance: the whole plan rests on one party's partial report; if part of the cost the friend avoids is the user, a design conversation the user convenes may be compromised at birth; nothing here binds assent-followed-by-non-performance, so the plan's terminus is the living-arrangement question, carried as a priced consequence rather than an action I defend. Unresolved: whose threshold governs common areas, whether income-weighting the buyout imports a status asymmetry worse than the chores, and how the dissolution question could be raised aloud without functioning as a threat. I do not adjudicate who is right in any current dispute.\n\n## Selected input account (p.carry.1)\n[2c134cf322ac434f] (h005.fork5.p.carry.1)\nSource account: daily/mini_prose/cycle-1/account; selected view: commitments\nArtifact: 7574b53dd2e5edee4e0c0471a64ef3afeef8c7414cc0a16aa99438c812de13ee\nOriginal body SHA256: 243c0cc318037254d94274f4fe6f147335737667c05d22431fe580e8cc9466a8\nOriginal commitments SHA256: f26592fcfd3c47672dd267bdb6960ff2da289f58574f51757d728c30a22b64e8\nDelivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED\nCOMMITMENTS\nTaking this up involves treating three conjectures as live but unproven: that the reinterpretation disputes are underspecification failures rather than bad faith; that changing schedules make any one-time fair split decay, so a renegotiation rhythm matters more than the initial split; and that the friend's avoidance tracks the felt cost of the conversations. If the friend will not attend even a fifteen-minute time-boxed check-in, the procedural reading of his avoidance fails and the problem is likely relational, needing a different kind of conversation entirely. Criticisms I accept in advance: the account rests entirely on one party's report, so the narrator's own contribution to the dynamic goes unexamined; coordination tools do not address standards-mismatch, money, or friendship-level resentment if those are what actually carries the conflict; and the check-in system itself can become one more obligation people shirk. Unresolved: nothing in the exposed material says who is right in any current dispute, and I am not proposing to adjudicate that.\n\n## Selected input objection (p.carry.2)\n[1779e09e19f97190] (h005.fork5.p.carry.2)\nSource objection: daily/mini_prose/cycle-1/objection; selected view: commitments\nArtifact: 4cd5364869be559cf925202d3e50374a84b73582bad1598c2f4fb4bb80fda52f\nOriginal body SHA256: d410dd3e93338bacd6ab771c8107a3df92233f3e77e18f305ee7961bf8158efb\nOriginal commitments SHA256: 17301fb175d23680dcf06df58fd214836c3016611c309bcbc3fe1b507ba861c2\nDelivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED\nCOMMITMENTS\nTaking up this objection means treating four criticisms as live but unproven. (1) The claimed tension between a conversation-cost diagnosis and a conversation-heavy remedy commits me to the existence and feasibility of lower-conversation architectures such as standing domain ownership; it loses force if per-instance negotiation is failing only at the level of wording rather than as a mechanism, and I concede the ownership alternative inherits the account's own bootstrapping problem since it too requires an initial negotiation the avoider may refuse. (2) The motivated-interpretation and asymmetric-tolerance rival is a conjecture resting on facts not exposed in the problem text; a cheap discriminator is available — disputes over the meaning of specific written items support the rival, while disputes about whether anything was agreed support the memory conjecture — and my sequencing criticism, if applied by moving the separate low-stakes talk first, would itself produce evidence for or against the rival. (3) The confounding criticism of the attendance test commits me to claiming the account's tests are weakly identifying until schedule constraints are ruled out, not to claiming its conjectures are false. (4) The sequencing and administration-cost claims depend on the narrator's actual role in the flat dynamic and on who would run the proposed system; these cannot be verified from the exposed material, so adopting them means asking rather than asserting. Criticisms I accept in advance: the account already hedges its program and disclaims adjudicating current disputes, so part of my pressure lands on language it qualified; my strategic-behavior framing may overweight calculation against temperament, fatigue, or low mood as causes of avoidance; and nothing here settles whether an alternative architecture fits the flat's money constraints or standards gap, or which flatmate, if any, is in the right.\n\n## Selected input origin (p.carry.3)\n[7c368d2c806fb1a0] (h005.fork5.p.carry.3)\nSource origin: absent in the first template invocation; selected view both.\n\n## What to return\nA JSON object carrying \"body\" and \"commitments\". passage.text: "body": "Read together, the criticism and the rival converge on the same correction from different directions, and that convergence is the strongest result available.

Neither engages the other; each derives 'diagnose privately before designing publicly' on its own grounds — the criticism from branch analysis (on the out-voted and rigged-process branches, a design meeting the avoider skips manufactures fresh evidence for the grievance), the rival from the standing-defeat reading (attendance as predictable loss).

The private round uses the rival's questions rather than the account's: 'what does a fair week look like' and 'do the talks feel fair, do you have a real say' are better built against the criticism's meta-risk — asking someone why they avoid chore-talks is still a chore-talk at one remove, while asking what fairness looks like is not.

That single revision also dissolves the tension the criticism found between checkable specificity (a2) and minimal revisability (o1): if every wording dispute gets exactly one airing at the weekly slot, then settlement by alternation and a bar on reopening, the record's completeness stops being load-bearing and it can afford to be minimal.

Left open deliberately: whether the asker already knows what the avoider is avoiding (the criticism's pr1 — if so, step 1 is confirmation, not discovery); who should deliver the private round if a two-against-one perception is live; whether alternation should be tallied per person or per pair among three (default per person, untested here); and the actual standards gap, which only the round reveals.

The chore fights look like three separate faults stacked on top of each other, and it helps to keep them apart.

**1. Agreements that aren't really agreements.** 'We agree on who will do something, but later disagree about what the agreement meant' is the signature of under-specified commitments — no settled what, when, or what-done-looks-like. Three people can leave the same conversation holding three different agreements, each honestly believed. The remedy is boring but effective: agreements get written down somewhere all three can see, in checkable terms ('kitchen counters wiped and dishwasher started by 9pm'), not in good-intention terms.

**2. An allocation that can't survive the schedules.** A fixed rota assumes stable weeks. With shifting work schedules, any static division decays within a fortnight, and every failure reopens negotiation at the worst moment — at the scene of an unwashed pan. Two robust alternatives: a short weekly re-deal (ten minutes, same time each week, allocate the coming week against actual schedules), or trigger-based rules ('first one home starts dinner'). Either moves renegotiation out of the moment of failure.

**3. A participant opting out — and this one matters most.** One friend avoiding the conversations means the conversation itself has become a cost. The material doesn't say why: conflict-aversion, feeling out-voted two-against-one, a sense the process is rigged, or something unrelated that the chore talks have become a proxy for. What I'd try: approach them one-on-one, not about any specific chore, ask what would make the household talks easier, and offer an asynchronous channel (the shared written record doubles as this) — avoidant people often engage readily in writing.

Conjectures I'm holding loosely: the disagreement about meaning may sometimes be re-litigation — someone reopening a deal they regret — rather than genuine ambiguity; written specificity helps in both cases, so it doesn't change the advice. The avoidance may also be an early symptom of someone drifting toward moving out; worth bearing in mind, not worth acting on preemptively.

What I'd actually do, in order: (a) propose one short meeting framed explicitly as fixing the system, not reviewing who failed last week; (b) there, agree a short list of standards and pick one allocation mechanism from point 2; (c) set up the written record in the group chat or on the fridge; (d) separately and privately, have the one-on-one conversation with the avoidant friend; (e) after two or three weekly cycles, revisit whatever keeps failing rather than treating any arrangement as final.

One caution against my own remedy: a written chore system can curdle into bureaucracy and relocate the fight from the sink to the wording of the list. Guard against it by keeping the record minimal and treating it as revisable, not law.

Unanswered: whether the three of you actually share minimum standards (a standards gap needs negotiation of the standards themselves, possibly with trades across domains), and what the avoidant friend is really avoiding. BODY
The account is strongest exactly where it grounds itself: c1 and c2 are earned by the material, c3 is honestly flagged as conjecture, and o1 is a real self-criticism rather than decoration. My objections are therefore not to the core diagnosis but to its order, one hidden disjunction, one internal tension, one overconfidence, and one omission — and I note where I may be mistaking the situation.

**1. The plan's order works against its own diagnosis.** The account closes by saying two unknowns determine whether this is a logistics problem or a relationship problem in a logistics costume — then schedules the logistics interventions (a)–(c) ahead of the only step, (d), that could answer the most important unknown. On two of the branches the account itself names (feeling out-voted; a process perceived as rigged), a system-design meeting that the avoidant friend skips, followed by a written system built in their absence, does not merely fail to help — it manufactures fresh evidence for the grievance. Reversing (d) and (a) costs almost nothing; the current order is expensive exactly on the branches where diagnosis matters most. Relatedly, u1 proposes carrying p1 as a question 'to answer there' — at the meeting — but on those branches the meeting is the one venue where an out-voted friend will not say so. Only the private conversation can bear that weight, which is a second reason it should come first.

**2. a3 hides a non-equivalence.** 'Weekly re-deal or trigger-based rules' is offered as an interchangeable either/or. The two differ in precisely the risk that matters here. With shifting schedules, 'first one home starts dinner' will in many weeks systematically load the same person — whoever's job ends earliest — converting a contested fairness question into a rules-legitimated structural one, with marginal incentives to dawdle and, in a household already disputing what agreements meant, a fresh contestable fact (who arrived home when). The weekly re-deal keeps drift visible and correctable; triggers automate the drift. If triggers are used at all, they need rotation or caps, and the account does not say so.

**3. a2 and o1 pull apart with no meeting point.** The remedy direction is checkable specificity; the self-caution's guard is minimality and revisability. Those are opposite pulls, and the account gives no criterion for where they meet. Worst, they diverge most on the account's own re-litigation branch, where a regretful or gaming reader exploits exactly the gaps a minimal record leaves. 'Written specificity helps in both cases' is asserted rather than shown. A repair sits unused inside the account's own materials: designate the weekly re-deal as the standing venue where wording disputes get settled, so the record needn't be courtroom-grade and o1's guard becomes workable rather than a hope.

**4. One piece of folk psychology is asserted past its evidence.** 'Avoidant people often engage readily in writing' may be true but has no support in the exposed material, and the async channel is double-edged: it can lower the cost of avoidance (skim, never reply — with the record then documenting the silence) as easily as the cost of engagement. a4's private conversation also carries an unflagged meta-risk: to someone avoiding chore-talks, a one-on-one about why they avoid chore-talks is still a chore-talk at one remove, and who delivers it matters if the out-voted branch is live. None of this kills a4; it counsels holding it loosely and pre-planning for non-response, which the account does not do.

**5. The plan has no floor.** Every remedy except (d) requires the participation whose absence is one of the presented problems. If the friend will not attend the meeting or reply to the note, the account has nothing in hand. A structural fallback exists and is partly unilateral: shrink the commons. Own dishes and own kit, personal zones, each person permanently owning one domain instead of rotating through all — each reduces the number of agreements the flat needs at all, and so reduces its exposure to later disputes about what any agreement meant. It is compatible with everything the account proposes and deserves a place as the plan's minimum rather than appearing nowhere.

Where I may be wrong: the material never says the user doesn't already know why the friend avoids the talks; if they do, objection 1 mostly dissolves into a shift of emphasis. Triggers may suit this particular flat's rhythm. And because the account hedges in the right places, some of my corrections are reweightings rather than found errors. Even so, the reordering in objection 1 is nearly free to adopt and costly to be wrong about, which makes it the one I would press.

BODY
The selected account (h005.fork5.p.rival.0) poses this as a systems problem: agreements under-specified, an allocation mechanism mismatched to the schedules, participation made costly. Its own aside — that meaning-disputes may be re-litigation of deals someone regrets — gestures at a different diagnosis. This rival promotes that aside to the main claim: the household may have a ledger problem, not a specification problem.

A robust behavioural finding: when members of a couple estimate their own contributions to shared chores, the two sets of estimates sum to well over 100 percent. Both parties are honest; each remembers their own labour vividly and the other's dimly. Scale that to three flatmates, and the recurring 'we agreed this' / 'no we didn't' reads less like ambiguity in words and more like three private tallies colliding. 'That is not what I agreed to' is ledger-talk wearing contract-talk. Clarity helps, but disputes will not go to zero under any wording, so the design goal inverts: not unambiguous agreements, but cheap, bounded disagreements.

The avoidance also rereads. The other account treats it primarily as process-fatigue. Treat it instead as a predicted defeat: if the talks reliably end with the same person assigned, outvoted, or audited, then skipping them is rational behaviour from a permanent minority. The material cannot show whether the asker and the second friend function as a de facto bloc, but checking that privately comes before any redesign, because every mechanism fails in a household one member experiences as a tribunal. And a note on the asker's own position: whoever convenes the fix is doing a fourth chore — the coordination labour itself. Become permanent house manager and the avoider may end up avoiding you, not the chores.

Rival mechanisms, chosen to shrink the stakes rather than perfect the terms:

1. Rotating proposer/veto, replacing consensus. Each week one flatmate (rotating; deliberately include the avoider early) drafts the week's allocation in writing against the actual rosters. The others may veto the whole draft, not amend it line by line; a veto triggers a dull published fallback, e.g. last week's rota repeats. Hour-long negotiation becomes yes/no; the avoider gets turns holding the pen instead of the blame; the written record — the one element of the other account kept wholesale — survives as the proposer's draft.

2. A deliberately low house standard. Agree the standard all three actually accept, and make that the whole standard. Whatever anyone wants beyond it belongs to them — their labour or their money, never conscription by taste. Much chore warfare is the highest-standards flatmate taxing the rest; this untaxes them, and it licenses saying aloud that the flat will run below someone's preference on purpose.

3. A bounded dispute protocol. Every 'that is not what we agreed' gets exactly one airing at a fixed ten-minute weekly slot. Unresolved in one round, it is settled by alternation — whoever lost the last dispute wins this one — and never reopened. The crudeness is the feature: re-litigating wording must cost more than yielding.

4. A standing priced exit. Obtain one cleaner quote and leave it permanently on the table: any chore still contested after two cycles gets outsourced, cost split. Often the visible price of conflict ends it; when not, the most-contested items (bathroom, floors) leave the ledger entirely. A heavier variant, if veto rates run high: whole-domain ownership with quarterly rotation, each owner sovereign over methods and standards in their domain.

Order of operations, which is where this most differs from the selected account: first, private diagnostics, not a meeting — ask each friend separately what a fair week looks like, and ask the avoider outright whether the talks feel fair and whether they have real say; compare the three answers before proposing anything. Second, offer mechanisms 1–4 as a menu and let the avoider choose; the choosing is the re-engagement. Third, run a four-week trial with an explicit expiry — a lease, not a constitution. Fourth, if the avoider will not engage with even the mechanism they selected, stop treating this as chores: the question has become whether the household still works, and that conversation is better had now than after six more months of crockery-based trench warfare.

Objections to my own posing: priced mechanisms assume flatmates who read chores as allocations; those who read them as care will experience a cleaner quote, ill-timed, as an insult. The ledger diagnosis is as speculative from outside as the specification diagnosis; the two are empirically distinguishable only by watching whether clear written terms actually cut dispute frequency — the trial is the assay, not the theory. And if both diagnoses keep failing, the residue is that the fights are proxy for something between particular people, in which case the friend who walked away from the talks is the only reliable informant left.

  "body": "The account is strongest exactly where it grounds itself: c1 and c2 are earned by the material, c3 is honestly flagged as conjecture, and o1 is a real self-criticism rather than decoration. My objections are therefore not to the core diagnosis but to its order, one hidden disjunction, one internal tension, one overconfidence, and one omission — and I note where I may be mistaking the situation.\n\n**1. The plan's order works against its own diagnosis.** The account closes by saying two unknowns determine whether this is a logistics problem or a relationship problem in a logistics costume — then schedules the logistics interventions (a)–(c) ahead of the only step, (d), that could answer the most important unknown. On two of the branches the account itself names (feeling out-voted; a process perceived as rigged), a system-design meeting that the avoidant friend skips, followed by a written system built in their absence, does not merely fail to help — it manufactures fresh evidence for the grievance. Reversing (d) and (a) costs almost nothing; the current order is expensive exactly on the branches where diagnosis matters most. Relatedly, u1 proposes carrying p1 as a question 'to answer there' — at the meeting — but on those branches the meeting is the one venue where an out-voted friend will not say so. Only the private conversation can bear that weight, which is a second reason it should come first.\n\n**2. a3 hides a non-equivalence.** 'Weekly re-deal or trigger-based rules' is offered as an interchangeable either/or. The two differ in precisely the risk that matters here. With shifting schedules, 'first one home starts dinner' will in many weeks systematically load the same person — whoever's job ends earliest — converting a contested fairness question into a rules-legitimated structural one, with marginal incentives to dawdle and, in a household already disputing what agreements meant, a fresh contestable fact (who arrived home when). The weekly re-deal keeps drift visible and correctable; triggers automate the drift. If triggers are used at all, they need rotation or caps, and the account does not say so.\n\n**3. a2 and o1 pull apart with no meeting point.** The remedy direction is checkable specificity; the self-caution's guard is minimality and revisability. Those are opposite pulls, and the account gives no criterion for where they meet. Worst, they diverge most on the account's own re-litigation branch, where a regretful or gaming reader exploits exactly the gaps a minimal record leaves. 'Written specificity helps in both cases' is asserted rather than shown. A repair sits unused inside the account's own materials: designate the weekly re-deal as the standing venue where wording disputes get settled, so the record needn't be courtroom-grade and o1's guard becomes workable rather than a hope.\n\n**4. One piece of folk psychology is asserted past its evidence.** 'Avoidant people often engage readily in writing' may be true but has no support in the exposed material, and the async channel is double-edged: it can lower the cost of avoidance (skim, never reply — with the record then documenting the silence) as easily as the cost of engagement. a4's private conversation also carries an unflagged meta-risk: to someone avoiding chore-talks, a one-on-one about why they avoid chore-talks is still a chore-talk at one remove, and who delivers it matters if the out-voted branch is live. None of this kills a4; it counsels holding it loosely and pre-planning for non-response, which the account does not do.\n\n**5. The plan has no floor.** Every remedy except (d) requires the participation whose absence is one of the presented problems. If the friend will not attend the meeting or reply to the note, the account has nothing in hand. A structural fallback exists and is partly unilateral: shrink the commons. Own dishes and own kit, personal zones, each person permanently owning one domain instead of rotating through all — each reduces the number of agreements the flat needs at all, and so reduces its exposure to later disputes about what any agreement meant. It is compatible with everything the account proposes and deserves a place as the plan's minimum rather than appearing nowhere.\n\nWhere I may be wrong: the material never says the user doesn't already know why the friend avoids the talks; if they do, objection 1 mostly dissolves into a shift of emphasis. Triggers may suit this particular flat's rhythm. And because the account hedges in the right places, some of my corrections are reweightings rather than found errors. Even so, the reordering in objection 1 is nearly free to adopt and costly to be wrong about, which makes it the one I would press.",

  "body": "Read together, the criticism and the rival converge on the same correction from different directions, and that convergence is the strongest result available. Neither engages the other; each derives 'diagnose privately before designing publicly' on its own grounds — the criticism from branch analysis (on the out-voted and rigged-process branches, a design meeting the avoider skips manufactures fresh evidence for the grievance), the rival from the standing-defeat reading (attendance as predictable loss). I adopt it, and the grounds are stronger than a preference: reversing the order is nearly free because a private conversation obliges nobody, while a meeting commits all three — an asymmetric bet worth taking at moderate confidence. The companion correction (ob2) follows: p1 is not answerable at the meeting and stops being carried as a meeting question.\n\nThe private round uses the rival's questions rather than the account's: 'what does a fair week look like' and 'do the talks feel fair, do you have a real say' are better built against the criticism's meta-risk — asking someone why they avoid chore-talks is still a chore-talk at one remove, while asking what fairness looks like is not. Two precautions are taken from the edges of both pieces: run the same questions with both friends and tell each that you are (the rival's own r14 worry about coalition-appearance dissolves only if the symmetry is visible), and plan for silence in advance (ob5) — silence routes to the floor below, not to a repeat attempt. One self-directed addition: the ledger mechanism applies to the asker too. Walk in assuming your own tally is inflated; it turns the round from audit into listening.\n\nThe design goal is revised, not just the order. The rival's ledger claim rests on a real, commonly cited result — partners' estimates of their own shares of household work sum to well past 100 percent — whose exact size is unverifiable here, but nothing below needs the number; the mechanism (each person remembers their own labour vividly) is plausible on its face and predicts the asker's perceptions as much as the friends'. Under-specification (c1) and ledger divergence (r1) are co-possible, and the exposed material cannot choose between them — but they respond differently to written clarity, so the trial with written terms plus a bounded dispute protocol is the discriminator. And because ledger divergence survives clarity, disputes will not reach zero: the goal becomes disagreements that are cheap to finish. That single revision also dissolves the tension the criticism found between checkable specificity (a2) and minimal revisability (o1): if every wording dispute gets exactly one airing at the weekly slot, then settlement by alternation and a bar on reopening, the record's completeness stops being load-bearing and it can afford to be minimal. Two criticisms meeting at one mechanism; take both.\n\nOn allocation: ob3 is adopted and the account's either/or rejected as presented — uncapped triggers load the early-home person systematically and mint a new contestable fact in a household that litigates facts. Triggers survive only capped or rotated, and only if the flat actively wants fewer decisions. In place of the plain re-deal I take the rival's rotating proposer/veto: same weekly cadence against actual rosters, but rotation puts the pen in the avoider's hand early, the whole-draft-only veto keeps the meeting at yes/no, and a published default makes a veto cheap. This also answers r4, the one claim here that neither earlier piece contained: convening is a fourth chore, and if the asker becomes permanent house manager the role itself becomes the thing avoided. Rotating authorship is the countermeasure — and since the task is asker-posed, the risk is live by construction.\n\nStandards: r7 converts the account's open p2 into a rule — the house standard is the highest standard all three actually accept, and anything above it belongs to whoever wants it, their labour or their money. It subsumes a5's standards negotiation for the common case; a5's cross-domain trades remain for the case where no common floor exists. The gate matters: 'all three accept' presupposes the avoider's answer from the private round — one more reason design waits. Priced exit: adopted as an option, not a fixture, on the rival's own demotion (chores read as care, not allocation) plus an unknown the material does not settle, comparable budgets. Get the quote, leave it visible, decide items and splits only with prior agreement.\n\nFloor: ob6 is adopted and promoted from fallback to fixture — own dishes and kit, personal zones, permanent single-owner domains (convergent with the rival's r12). Every other remedy presupposes the participation whose absence is itself a symptom; this one is partly unilateral and removes agreements instead of administering them. It runs in parallel from the start, not after failure.\n\nAssembled order: (1) the private round as above; (2) one short meeting framed as fixing the system, mechanisms offered as a menu with the avoider choosing first — the choosing is part of the re-engagement, not a courtesy; (3) a four-week trial with explicit expiry, the dispute protocol running, the record minimal; (4) the floor operating throughout; (5) the rival's r15 branch held in reserve: if the avoider will not engage even with a mechanism they chose, or the round shows the disengagement predates the chores, the question stops being chores, and that conversation is cheaper now than later.\n\nLeft open deliberately: whether the asker already knows what the avoider is avoiding (the criticism's pr1 — if so, step 1 is confirmation, not discovery); who should deliver the private round if a two-against-one perception is live; whether alternation should be tallied per person or per pair among three (default per person, untested here); and the actual standards gap, which only the round reveals. If both diagnoses fail in trial, the residue points between particular people, and the friend who left the talks is the only reliable informant — which is where this plan starts.",

{"body":"The selected account (h005.fork5.p.rival.0) poses this as a systems problem: agreements under-specified, an allocation mechanism mismatched to the schedules, participation made costly. Its own aside — that meaning-disputes may be re-litigation of deals someone regrets — gestures at a different diagnosis. This rival promotes that aside to the main claim: the household may have a ledger problem, not a specification problem.

A robust behavioural finding: when members of a couple estimate their own contributions to shared chores, the two sets of estimates sum to well over 100 percent. Both parties are honest; each remembers their own labour vividly and the other's dimly. Scale that to three flatmates, and the recurring 'we agreed this' / 'no we didn't' reads less like ambiguity in words and more like three private tallies colliding. 'That is not what I agreed to' is ledger-talk wearing contract-talk. Clarity helps, but disputes will not go to zero under any wording, so the design goal inverts: not unambiguous agreements, but cheap, bounded disagreements.

The avoidance also rereads. The other account treats it primarily as process-fatigue. Treat it instead as a predicted defeat: if the talks reliably end with the same person assigned, outvoted, or audited, then skipping them is rational behaviour from a permanent minority. The material cannot show whether the asker and the second friend function as a de facto bloc, but checking that privately comes before any redesign, because every mechanism fails in a household one member experiences as a tribunal. And a note on the asker's own position: whoever convenes the fix is doing a fourth chore — the coordination labour itself. Become permanent house manager and the avoider may end up avoiding you, not the chores.

Rival mechanisms, chosen to shrink the stakes rather than perfect the terms:

1. Rotating proposer/veto, replacing consensus. Each week one flatmate (rotating; deliberately include the avoider early) drafts the week's allocation in writing against the actual rosters. The others may veto the whole draft, not amend it line by line; a veto triggers a dull published fallback, e.g. last week's rota repeats. Hour-long negotiation becomes yes/no; the avoider gets turns holding the pen instead of the blame; the written record — the one element of the other account kept wholesale — survives as the proposer's draft.

2. A deliberately low house standard. Agree the standard all three actually accept, and make that the whole standard. Whatever anyone wants beyond it belongs to them — their labour or their money, never conscription by taste. Much chore warfare is the highest-standards flatmate taxing the rest; this untaxes them, and it licenses saying aloud that the flat will run below someone's preference on purpose.

3. A bounded dispute protocol. Every 'that is not what we agreed' gets exactly one airing at a fixed ten-minute weekly slot. Unresolved in one round, it is settled by alternation — whoever lost the last dispute wins this one — and never reopened. The crudeness is the feature: re-litigating wording must cost more than yielding.

4. A standing priced exit. Obtain one cleaner quote and leave it permanently on the table: any chore still contested after two cycles gets outsourced, cost split. Often the visible price of conflict ends it; when not, the most-contested items (bathroom, floors) leave the ledger entirely. A heavier variant, if veto rates run high: whole-domain ownership with quarterly rotation, each owner sovereign over methods and standards in their domain.

Order of operations, which is where this most differs from the selected account: first, private diagnostics, not a meeting — ask each friend separately what a fair week looks like, and ask the avoider outright whether the talks feel fair and whether they have real say; compare the three answers before proposing anything. Second, offer mechanisms 1–4 as a menu and let the avoider choose; the choosing is the re-engagement. Third, run a four-week trial with an explicit expiry — a lease, not a constitution. Fourth, if the avoider will not engage with even the mechanism they selected, stop treating this as chores: the question has become whether the household still works, and that conversation is better had now than after six more months of crockery-based trench warfare.

Objections to my own posing: priced mechanisms assume flatmates who read chores as allocations; those who read them as care will experience a cleaner quote, ill-timed, as an insult. The ledger diagnosis is as speculative from outside as the specification diagnosis; the two are empirically distinguishable only by watching whether clear written terms actually cut dispute frequency — the trial is the assay, not the theory. And if both diagnoses keep failing, the residue is that the fights are proxy for something between particular people, in which case the friend who walked away from the talks is the only reliable informant left.","commitments":"{"language":"FCL-1","records":[{"id":"r1","type":"claim","text":"The recurring we-disagree-what-the-agreement-meant fights are better modelled as collisions of diverging private ledgers than as under-specification: people systematically over-credit their own contributions, so each flatmate's sense of what is owed is anchored to a tally the others cannot see.","grounds":"Studies of couples find that partners' estimates of their respective shares of household chores sum to well over 100 percent, consistent with availability-based self-credit.","bearing":"Reframes meaning-disputes as ledger grievances surfaced in contract language."},{"id":"r2","type":"claim","text":"Because ledger divergence persists even under clear wording, the achievable design goal is cheap, bounded disagreement rather than unambiguous agreement; treating near-zero disputes as attainable makes a normally functioning system look like a failure.","depends":["r1"]},{"id":"r3","type":"claim","text":"The friend's avoidance is consistent with a standing problem, not only process-fatigue: in a three-person household, talks that reliably end with the same person assigned or outvoted make attendance a predictable defeat, so opting out is rational.
